claim: CORE-Bench defines correctness by comparing agent answers with repeated manual reproductions.
quote: We determine if an agent correctly solves a task if the agent's reported results for all questions fall within a 95% prediction interval for every task question of the results from the three manual runs (although only 17 / 181 task questions have stochastic answers).

claim: Its authors note that building on public repositories allows periodic updates.
quote: CORE-Bench's foundation in public repositories enables periodic updates of the benchmark tasks, which could mitigate concerns about contamination and saturation.

claim: A later case study of CORE-Bench reports that it surfaced threats to construct validity in CORE-Bench Hard that are difficult to anticipate with less capable agents.
quote: First, we surface threats to construct validity in CORE-Bench Hard that are difficult to anticipate with less capable agents.

claim: PaperBench uses an LLM-based judge to automatically grade replication attempts against rubrics.
quote: we also develop an LLM-based judge to automatically grade replication attempts against rubrics

claim: Its best judge reached an F1 of 0.83 against human gold labels.
quote: Our best LLM-based judge, which uses o3-mini-high with custom scaffolding, achieves an F1 score of 0.83 on the auxiliary evaluation, suggesting that this judge is a reasonable stand-in for a human judge.

claim: The authors themselves say more work is needed on judge accuracy.
quote: We've taken an early step with JudgeEval (Section 4.2) to measure the accuracy of model-based judges on tasks with huge complex outputs, but more work is needed to improve accuracy and understand their strengths and weaknesses.
locator: sec. A.2. Improving automated judges, para 104

claim: SciReplicate-Bench argues that PaperBench and Paper2CodeBench rely substantially on manual assessment criteria and LLM-based correctness judgments, introducing potential inconsistencies and reliability concerns.
quote: these evaluation approaches rely substantially on manual assessment criteria and LLM-based correctness judgments, introducing potential inconsistencies and reliability concerns.
locator: sec. Our work makes the following contributions:, para 5

claim: SciReplicate-Bench states that its recent publication window was deliberately chosen to minimize the risk of data leakage.
quote: This recent publication window was deliberately chosen to minimize the risk of data leakage.

claim: One study finds that pairwise LLM-judge preferences flip across identical runs: on average 13.6% of the time.
quote: Across judges, pairwise preferences flip on average 13.6% of the time, with 28% of questions exceeding a 20% flip rate and one question reaching 56%.

claim: Another reports that exact-match agreement overstates judge ability.
quote: LLM-as-a-Judge has become the dominant evaluation paradigm for language models, but judge validation in practice relies on exact-match agreement, a metric that does not correct for chance and systematically overstates discriminative ability.

claim: A survey of AI-scientist systems finds LLM-as-judge is the most common evaluator.
quote: Second, LLM-as-judge is the most common evaluator across the corpus, so most outputs remain candidates rather than findings;

claim: Another study reports that across six judges, small prompt design choices have large consequences for novelty verdicts.
quote: Across six judges, we find that small prompt design choices have large consequences;

claim: HindSight reports that LLM-judged novelty correlates negatively with future-impact scores.
quote: Moreover, HindSight scores are \emph{negatively} correlated with LLM-judged novelty ($ρ{=}{-}0.29$, $p{<}0.01$), suggesting that LLMs systematically overvalue novel-sounding ideas that never materialize in real research.

claim: OpenNovelty instead grounds assessments in retrieved prior work.
quote: Unlike naive LLM-based approaches, \textsc{OpenNovelty} grounds all assessments in retrieved real papers, ensuring verifiable judgments.

claim: The human ideation study acknowledges that human judgements of novelty can be difficult, even by experts.
quote: we acknowledge that human judgements of novelty can be difficult, even by experts

claim: On variance, a clinical-agent study notes that benchmarks usually score one run per task.
quote: benchmarks typically score one run per task and rarely ask whether identical inputs produce identical actions;

claim: FIRE-Bench reports high variance across runs.
quote: even the strongest agents achieve limited rediscovery success (<50 F1), exhibit high variance across runs, and display recurring failure modes in experimental design, execution, and evidence-based reasoning.

claim: A contamination survey cautions that an LLM used for automatic evaluation may itself be contaminated.
quote: Automatic evaluation can mitigate some effects of BDC by employing self-supervised methods that reduce reliance on labeled data, but this approach cannot completely eliminate the risk of contamination, for example, the LLM used for automatic evaluation may also suffers from the BDC problem.
